Market Research Hub

Real data and worked research paths for the People section of your business plan: Geographics, Demographics, Psychographics, and Business Landscape.

Market research doesn't start with a blank Google search

The foundation of your business plans are the 5 P's: Product, Price, Promotion, Place, and People. Each one of these areas needs careful consideration as you build your business. Market research lets you know if you are on the right track. This site is a hub for market research so you can answer core questions about your potential customers, your competitors, and the trends that will make or break your business.

The four parts of People

Click a card to jump to that tab. Geographics and Demographics share one tab, since they're both pulled from the same Census data.

Data-backed vs. hypothesis

  • Every claim in your pitch should end up tagged one of two ways.
  • Data-backed means it comes from a real, cited source: the Demographics tab, or one of the sources on the Psychographics and Business Landscape tabs.
  • Hypothesis means it's an informed guess, built from the closest available data, waiting to be tested with real customers later in the year.
  • Keeping that distinction visible (a simple two-column table works) is good practice for any pitch, and it's honest about what you actually know versus what you're betting on.
American Community Survey · 5-Year Estimates, 2020–2024

Demographics

Real Census data for Geographics and Demographics, plus the household-economics side of Business Landscape: population, income, education, housing, mobility, and more for San Francisco neighborhoods, Bay Area counties, California, and the nation.

Where this data comes from, and what "5-year estimate" means

This isn't a full count like the once-a-decade Census. It's the American Community Survey (ACS), a continuous household survey the Census Bureau mails, calls, and knocks on doors for, all year, every year. About 3.5 million addresses are randomly selected nationwide each year, with roughly 1.9 million completed interviews, on the order of 1 in 65 households in a given year. Scaled to San Francisco's ~364,000 households, that works out to somewhere around 5,000–6,000 SF households a year, or roughly 25,000–30,000 over five years (our own estimate, scaled from the Bureau's national rate, not a published city-level figure).

"5-year estimate" means every number here is blended from interviews collected across all of 2020–2024, not a single-year snapshot. The Census Bureau does this because small areas (like a single SF neighborhood) don't get enough interviews in any one year to produce a reliable number on their own. Pooling five years of interviews together builds up a big enough sample, at the cost of the number reflecting a 5-year period rather than "right now." This tool uses 5-year estimates for every tier, including the nation and the state, so every geography is measured the same way and can be fairly compared.

Because it's a sample and not a full count, every estimate carries a margin of error: smaller areas (like an SF neighborhood) have wider margins than larger ones (like the nation). See the "margin of error" section below for what that means for the numbers you're looking at right now.

San Francisco neighborhoods are Census PUMAs (Public Use Microdata Areas), the smallest geography the ACS publishes detailed estimates for, each covering roughly 100,000–150,000 residents, so they group several real neighborhoods together rather than matching them one-to-one.

Psychographics · What do customers like outside of work?

Understanding how people spend their time and attention

No dataset answers "what does my customer like" directly. This is the category best confirmed later with real customer conversations. Until then, build an evidence-based persona from the sources below, and label every claim built from them as a hypothesis, not a fact.

Turning these into a persona claim

Every claim built from the sources below should read like a hypothesis, not a fact: "We believe our customers spend significant leisure time on Instagram, based on Pew's age-based usage data," not "our customers are on Instagram." Keep a simple two-column table in the business plan (Data-backed vs. Hypothesis) so it's clear which claims are measured and which are informed guesses waiting to be tested.

Business Landscape · Where do they shop, and who else is selling to them?

Spending capacity and the competitive landscape

The Demographics tab already covers income and rent: spending capacity. This tab covers spending behavior (how much of that capacity goes where) and the competitive landscape (who's already selling to them).

Business Landscape: who's already selling to them

Real County Business Patterns (CBP) data: how many businesses like yours already exist. Unlike the Demographics tab, CBP doesn't publish numbers below the county level, so there's no San Francisco neighborhood breakdown here.

San Francisco Neighborhoods: snapshot & trend

Real SF business-registration data (DataSF), broken out by the city's own ~40 planning neighborhoods. Note: these are not the same groupings as the "San Francisco" tier on the Demographics tab (which uses Census PUMAs), so don't cross-compare those numbers directly.
